summary: The note is a Wikipedia article defining a continent as a large geographical region identified by convention rather than strict criteria. It explains that the number of continents varies from four to seven depending on the model, covers the seven-continent model common in English-speaking countries, and discusses separation, geological continents, supercontinents, and the history of the concept from ancient Greek geography through European arrival in the Americas to the recognition of Antarctica and Australia as continents.
one_line: Wikipedia overview of what a continent is, how many continents are recognized under different models, and how the concept developed historically.
key_facts: A continent is any of several large geographical regions, generally identified by convention rather than strict criteria.
Up to seven or as few as four geographical regions are commonly regarded as continents.
Most English-speaking countries recognize seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia.
Australia, at 7,617,930 square kilometres, is deemed the smallest continent, while Greenland (2,166,086 square kilometres) is considered the world's largest island.
Of the seven most globally recognized continents, only Antarctica and Australia are completely separated from other continents by the ocean.
Geologists use four key attributes to define a continent: elevation, geology, crustal structure, and limits and area of more than one million square kilometres.
With the addition of Zealandia in 2017, Earth currently has seven recognized geological continents.
Herodotus in the 5th century BC questioned the division of the world into three continents, arguing Europe was larger than the other two combined.
Amerigo Vespucci's account Mundus Novus, published in 1502 or 1503, is the first known explicit identification of part of the Americas as a continent.
Martin Waldseemüller's 1507 world map Universalis Cosmographia was the first to show North and South America as separate from Asia.
The Rig Veda, often dated 1500 BCE, has the earliest mention of seven continents according to the article.
Europeans discovered Australia in 1606, and by the late 18th century some geographers considered it a continent in its own right.
Antarctica was sighted in 1820 during the First Russian Antarctic Expedition and described as a continent by Charles Wilkes in 1838.
Madagascar is referred to as "the eighth continent" from a biological perspective.

entities.role: continent joined to South America by the Isthmus of Panama in the seven-continent model

entities.role: continent in the seven-continent model, treated with North America as America in some models

entities.name: Antarctica
entities.role: continent described by Charles Wilkes in 1838 and the last continent identified

entities.name: Europe
entities.role: continent with a land area of 10,180,000 square kilometres, treated as separate from Asia in most categorizations

entities.name: Australia
entities.role: smallest continent by area, separated by ocean from other continents

entities.name: Oceania
entities.role: geographical region grouping Pacific island countries with the continent of Australia

entities.name: Zealandia
entities.role: submerged continent added as a geological continent in 2017

entities.name: Madagascar
entities.role: microcontinent usually considered an island of Africa, called the eighth continent from a biological perspective

entities.name: Pangaea
entities.role: supercontinent from which the current continents broke up, formed hundreds of millions of years ago

entities.name: Greenland
entities.role: world's largest island, not considered a continent

entities.name: Herodotus
entities.role: 5th century BC Greek writer who questioned dividing the world into three continents
